# Limits, open questions, and directions {#sec-limits}

ISLA has no measured accuracy advantage over GeoTransolver or Transolver
on surface pressure once every model receives the freestream at the same
unit scale (@sec-part-baseline). At 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases
GeoTransolver scores 0.111 and Transolver 0.115 against the reference
configuration's 0.1529 (0.73x and 0.75x, baseline ÷ ISLA; 0.80x and 0.83x
of the constant-gauge variant's 0.1377), and the baselines lead at every
other rung measured: GeoTransolver 0.83x at 210 cases, 0.84x at 510, 0.76x
at four training geometries, 0.92x at 21 and 0.78x at the fixed angle,
Transolver 0.91x at 210, 0.90x at 510, 0.77x at four geometries, 0.93x at
21 and 0.86x at the fixed angle (these ratios are against the
constant-gauge variant, which the reference trails
by 1–14.5% on the wings, so the ratios against the reference are lower
still). The 1,260-case rung is not yet measured with unit-drive baselines
(@sec-program-status). On DrivAerML at full data the released
GeoTransolver and Transolver score 0.0503 and 0.0517 against the
reference's 0.0552 in float32, and GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate
at every size below full data. What stands is a set of contracts that
GeoTransolver does not have; a 6% and 19% lead over the augmented
baselines when geometries arrive in arbitrary poses; a consistency
property, 1.2x degradation under a 10:1 sampling-density bias where every
configuration that centres on the sampled points degrades 10–16x; and an
interior standing of one lead in three fields (27% ahead on velocity, 7%
behind on pressure, 14% behind on eddy viscosity). This chapter states the
boundary of each claim as a fact about the evidence, lists the open
questions with the preregistered outcome that settles each, and names
what would change the recommendation.

## What is established {#sec-established}

Eight results are settled to the standard of the fair-comparison protocol
(@sec-protocol), and together they support the one-sentence verdict of
@sec-verdict. Each carries its numbers and its own scope statement in its
home section; this chapter adds only the limits.

- On HiLiftAeroML surface pressure, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the
  unit freestream direction match or beat ISLA at every rung measured: 35,
  210 and 510 random training cases, 4 and 21 training geometries, and the
  fixed angle (@sec-part-baseline, @sec-de-result). At 35 cases the
  baselines are lower on 130 and 152 of 180 cases; at 510 on 168 of 180.
  The 1,260-case rung has a physical-drive GeoTransolver only, at parity
  with the constant-gauge variant (0.0408 against 0.0405 in float32).
- On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cars up
  (@sec-de-drivaerml) and the released GeoTransolver and Transolver lead at
  full data, 0.0503 and 0.0517 against 0.0552 (@sec-full-data). The
  ladder was measured with GeoTransolver's physical-velocity input, which
  on this dataset is not a handicap: at 435 cars the unit-drive
  GeoTransolver scores 0.0503 against 0.0498 with the physical velocity.
- The pose contract: rotation and translation covariance exact by
  construction, with a finite-precision residual on the bf16 path that is
  measured rather than assumed (@sec-pose, @sec-mt2-contracts). With every
  case in its own random SO(3) pose, ISLA scores 0.0566 against 0.0602 for
  GeoTransolver with SO(3) augmentation and 0.0676 for Transolver with
  augmentation, a 6% and 19% lead in float32.
- Learning-rate robustness on DrivAerML (@sec-robustness-lr), and the cost
  of both models in one harness on the recipe's compiled path: at 10,000
  tokens ISLA's step is 1.05x GeoTransolver's (47 against 45 ms) at 1.30
  against 2.70 GiB with the geometry recompute on, 0.86x without it; at
  40,000 tokens 2.2x by default and parity with the exact fused geometry
  kernel (@sec-mt2-cost).
- Consistency: the reference frame degrades 1.2x under a 10:1
  sampling-density bias where every configuration that centres on the
  sampled points degrades 10–16x, and under refinement the measure-weighted
  ISLA's convention-swap penalty converges 2.9x → 1.45x → 1.05x from 2,500
  to 40,000 cells while the released baselines stay at 3–7x
  (@sec-robustness-density, @sec-consistency-bench).
- Interior accuracy: ISLA's reference configuration, query tokens with the
  signed distance, leads GeoTransolver-volume on interior velocity by 27%
  at a third of the parameters and trails on pressure (7%) and eddy
  viscosity (14%) in float32; the passive, query-independent decode trails
  by 3.1x (@sec-interior). GeoTransolver-volume fed the unit direction
  instead of the physical velocity changes by under 2% on every field, so
  the ordering stands against either (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict).
- Regime extrapolation: nothing tested generalizes across a flow-regime
  boundary (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- Cross-family transfer is a property of the training data for every
  architecture tested (@sec-limits-transfer).

## Limits of each headline claim {#sec-review-honesty}

### The HiLiftAeroML ladder: what its curves measure {#sec-limits-data-efficiency}

**Unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver lie below ISLA's curve at every
case-count rung measured, 35, 210 and 510 training cases, at a nearly
constant ratio; the 1,260-case rung has a physical-drive GeoTransolver
only.** The quantity throughout is the surface-pressure relative L2 error
as defined in @sec-metrics, averaged over the 180 validation cases shared
by every rung of the nested splits, in float32. Against the constant-gauge
variant of ISLA (0.1377 / 0.0643 / 0.0489 at 35 / 210 / 510 cases)
GeoTransolver scores 0.111 / 0.0539 / 0.0410 (0.80x / 0.84x / 0.84x, lower
on 130 / 161 / 168 of 180 cases) and Transolver 0.115 / 0.0578 / 0.0441
(0.83x / 0.90x / 0.90x). The reference configuration is trained at 35 and
210 cases and scores 0.1529 and 0.0716, 11% above the constant-gauge
variant at both rungs (@sec-limits-mechanism), so against it the
baselines' ratios are 0.73x and 0.75x at 35 cases and 0.75x and 0.81x at
210. At 1,260 cases the physical-drive GeoTransolver (0.0408) and the
constant-gauge variant (0.0405) are at parity; the unit-drive baseline at
that rung is not yet measured (@sec-program-status), and since the unit
drive has lowered every baseline number on every other rung, the parity is
a floor on the baseline's standing, not a ceiling. Every seed at a rung
trains on the same curated subset, so the seed bands measure
initialization, not the choice of training cases; geometry-stratified
redraws of the 35- and 210-case training sets put the GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA
ratio between 0.84 and 0.98 at 35 cases and between 0.82 and 0.93 at 210
(90% intervals over three draws), so the curated draws are typical and the
ordering holds on every draw.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ladder-unit-drive
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The HiLiftAeroML ladder with unit-drive baselines. Pressure relative L2
#|   error on the shared 180-case validation set versus number of training
#|   cases, log-log, float32, seed means with the individual seeds as small
#|   dots. Filled blue squares: ISLA, constant-gauge variant, at 35, 210, 510
#|   and 1,260 cases. Hollow blue diamonds: ISLA, reference configuration
#|   (relative frame, total-measure scale), at the two rungs it is trained
#|   on. Red circles: GeoTransolver fed the unit freestream direction, at its
#|   best learning rate per the protocol of @sec-protocol. Grey triangles:
#|   Transolver fed the unit direction. The hollow red circle at 1,260 cases
#|   is GeoTransolver fed the physical freestream velocity, the only baseline
#|   measured at that rung. How to read this: the baselines lie below both
#|   ISLA curves at every rung where they were run with the unit drive; it
#|   does not show a unit-drive baseline at 1,260 cases, which is not yet
#|   measured. Protocol: learning rate 1e-3 for ISLA and for GeoTransolver
#|   at 210 and above (3e-3 at 35 cases), 3e-3 for Transolver, 500 epochs,
#|   bfloat16 training, no augmentation, 10,000 sampled points per case.
#|   Data: results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json,
#|   results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
#|   results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json and
#|   results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json.
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)

INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"

R = Path("..") / "results"

def p32(*names):

isla_cg = {35: p32(*[f"lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]),
           210: p32(*[f"lad_hl_mt2_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]),

gt_unit = {35: p32("udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed42", "udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed43"),
           210: u210["gt_unit_lr1e3"]["seed_pressure"], 510: u510["gt_unit"]["seed_pressure"]}
tr_unit = {35: p32(*[f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]),

    xs = sorted(d); ms_ = [statistics.mean(d[x]) for x in xs]

ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
ax.set_xlim(25, 1800); ax.set_ylim(0.033, 0.2)

```

Three facts bound what the curves can say. The measurements are scoped to
the range in which every production CFD dataset in this program lives; no
scaling-law statement is made. ISLA's flattening toward 1,260 cases may be
a floor of the protocol rather than a property of ISLA: at 1,260 cases the
two architectures share 70% of their residual on identical points, the
correlation between two-seed disagreement and per-case error collapses for
both, and accuracy still rises with points per case (6,500 → 10,000 points
is worth 8% for ISLA), which is what a resolution or label floor looks like
(@sec-shared-floor). And the baselines' curve above 510 cases is not
measured with the unit drive, so whether the ratio of 0.84x holds, widens
or closes at 1,260 cases is the one open cell of the ladder
(@sec-open-questions).

### The HiLift accuracy figures are validation-set figures {#sec-limits-validation}

**Every HiLiftAeroML accuracy number in this book is scored on the shared
180-case validation set; the 360-case test set has not been spent on the
accuracy claims, and no HiLiftAeroML split remains that could confirm them
independently of the program's own history.** The protocol evaluates the
final-epoch checkpoint of every run, so no checkpoint is selected on
validation error. The validation set entered more than one decision: each
architecture's learning-rate choice on the full 1,260-case split
(@sec-lr-protocol), Transolver's learning-rate choice per small-data rung,
the design of the ablations that followed earlier readouts, and the choice of
which results to present. The ladder therefore carries no checkpoint-selection
optimism, but the learning rates were chosen on the same 180 cases (118
geometries) the ladder is scored on, and every control, ablation and
stratified readout in @sec-data-efficiency reads the same cases. The test
splits were spent only on regime extrapolation and the raw-coordinate
discriminator (@sec-regime-extrapolation, @sec-limits-regime), which train on
different splits. Those two evaluations, however, read 900 and 723 cases
that between them contain every one of the 180 geometries, and the
manifests overlap: the 360-case data-efficiency test set shares 179 cases
with them, the geometry test set 182 and the deflection test set 182, and
the latter two also share 37 and 40 cases with the validation set
(@sec-splits; results/hilift_exposure_ledger_2026-09-08.json). Every
remaining test split is therefore *held out per checkpoint*, since no model
trained on it, but not a *program-level confirmation*, since results on
overlapping cases have already informed the program's decisions; and
removing the already-read cases post hoc would define a new, selected
population, not a replacement confirmatory set. A sealed evaluation of the
35-case ISLA and unit-drive baseline checkpoints on the 360 test cases would
still be informative as a within-protocol held-out check of the 35-case
ratios (@sec-part-baseline), and is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status); an independent confirmation needs geometries no part
of the program has scored, which on HiLiftAeroML means a prospective
dataset.

### Mechanism: what is known about where the deficits come from {#sec-limits-mechanism}

**The input-scale requirement of the fair-comparison protocol is a fact
about the baselines: fed the physical freestream velocity,
GeoTransolver's global-context projector collapses to one occupied slice,
which costs it 3.4–3.8x at 35 cases (@sec-part-baseline). With the input
matched there is no ISLA advantage on surface pressure to explain at any
rung measured, and the deficits that remain are located: ISLA's surface
deficit is representational, the reference frame's price on the wings is
the mesher pattern the plain-mean frame carries, and the interior
standings sort into capacity and generalization.** The search of ISLA for
a load-bearing ingredient is informative about ISLA. Five single-factor
ablations at 35 cases (adding raw coordinates, which breaks the SE(3)
contract; replacing the invariant seeds by raw vectors; turning the
similarity gauge on; turning the measure weights off; removing the
relational routing from the encoder) each change its error by between −12%
and +16% (@sec-mechanism), so no single contract or channel is
load-bearing for ISLA's own accuracy, and the exactness of the SE(3)
contract neither costs nor buys anything measurable in distribution.
ISLA's own residual error on the wings concentrates in the gap regions
between the elements (59–71% of its squared error on the 15% of points
nearest another surface, @tbl-hilift-hlreg), which locates where ISLA's
output error sits, not what information produces it.

On DrivAerML, where the geometry variation is a smooth morph of one car,
the ladder protocol at a frozen learning rate of 3e-3 for both
architectures gives GeoTransolver the lead: the two are tied at 14 cases
(GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.99) and GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate
than ISLA at every rung from 27 to 218 cases (@tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder
in @sec-data-efficiency), with the physical velocity (38.9 m/s) as its
input; at 435 cars the unit-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.0503 against
0.0498 with the physical velocity, inside the null band
(@sec-nb-uw-verdict), so on DrivAerML the physical input is not a handicap
and the ladder's ordering stands. The shortfall is not located anywhere on
the car. Binning each validation case's 10,000 points into streamwise
thirds and taking the per-bin RMS pressure-error ratio ISLA ÷
GeoTransolver (medians over the 48 cases, two seed pairs), the rear third
reads 1.27 and 1.32 against the front third's 1.16 and 1.28; the
rear-to-front factor is 1.10 and 1.03, at or under the preregistered
falsification bar of 1.1
(results/drivaer_station_attribution_2026-09-07.json;
@sec-nb-drivaer-station-verdict). Both models put about 56–59% of their
squared error on the front third and about 20% on the rear; ISLA is
uniformly a little worse everywhere, and least worse on the middle third
(1.10, 1.12), so a wake-context extension would be aimed at a deficit the
data do not show. The two architectures agree on which cars are hard:
their per-case errors are rank-correlated at 0.86–0.89, the same as each
model with its own second seed (0.87), and the per-case ratio sits between
1.11 and 1.38 for 80% of cars, with GeoTransolver ahead on 47–48 of 48
(results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json). The gap is a
near-constant factor on a shared difficulty ordering.

On the geometry rungs of HiLiftAeroML the unit-drive baselines are ahead
too: GeoTransolver 0.1884 against the constant-gauge variant's 0.2496 from
four training geometries (0.76x by the mean; 9 of 18 held-out geometries
each way, so the geometry-level ordering is a tie and the case-level count,
96 of 180, is descriptive; @sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict), 0.0933 against
0.1014 from 21 geometries (0.92x; lower on 136 of 180 cases;
@sec-nb-udrvl-geo210-verdict), and 0.0270 against 0.0348 on the
fixed-angle split of 126 geometries at 12° validated on 18 geometries
never seen at any angle (0.78x; Transolver 0.86x; each ahead on 18 of 18
geometries; @sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict). What stands as a
fact about ISLA is that its error responds to the number of training
geometries (0.2496 at 4, 0.1014 at 21, 0.0348 at 126 at the fixed angle;
0.2520, 0.1066 and 0.0398 for the reference configuration), and that a
unit-drive GeoTransolver's error responds the same way (0.1884, 0.0933,
0.0270).

**ISLA's surface deficit is representational, not a shortage of training
cases.** The cleanest test of a data limit is to remove the data axis:
train each architecture on a single case, presented as 64 independent
10,000-cell views of the same surface, until its training loss stops
falling, and read the floor it reaches on a fresh resampling of that same
case (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict; float32; the arms carry the unit-drive
input, and the fp32-trained pair is the like-for-like comparison). If the
35-case gap were a data limit, the gap at one case should be smaller or
vanish; it is wider. On the HiLiftAeroML wing ISLA's single-case floor is
1.27x GeoTransolver's and 1.37x Transolver's in the bfloat16-trained arms
and 1.55x in the fp32-trained pair, against a 35-case gap of 1.11–1.20x
for the constant-gauge variant; on the DrivAerML car it is 1.31–1.39x,
over the preregistered 1.5x capacity bar in the fp32 pair. The same
ordering is visible in the training losses on ISLA's own views, so the gap
is present before any generalization question arises. Split by facing
distance, the deficit sits on the mid- and far-field open surfaces
(baseline ÷ ISLA 0.64–0.83) and is smallest at the gaps (0.88): the
missing capacity is on the smooth, large-cell regions that dominate the
area-weighted metric of @sec-metrics, not in gap physics.

**Measure weights are a correctness requirement whose in-distribution
price is estimator variance plus mesh-pattern content.** ISLA weights
each surface point by its cell area in the slice routing and the pooled
anchors, which is what makes its slice states estimates of surface
integrals and its predictions consistent under refinement
(@sec-consistency-bench). Under uniform-over-cells sampling the weights
cost accuracy in distribution: the weights-off ablation is 5–10% better at
35 HiLiftAeroML cases (draw-dependent), 8% at 210, 11% at 21 geometries,
17% at 4 geometries and 10.6% at the fixed angle, and 2.9% better on
DrivAerML; with the data fixed on a single case it is still 17% better on
both datasets, so the cost is representational, not a few-sample effect.
A forward-pass probe of the single-case checkpoints identifies the
mechanism as estimator variance (@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe).
Uniform-over-cells sampling draws a heavy tail of cell areas (4.4% of the
wing's cells carry half the sampled area), and a quadrature-weighted mean
over such a draw has an effective sample size of $N/(1+\mathrm{CV}^2)$ of
the areas: 862 of 9,983 wing cells, 1,637 of 10,000 car cells. The learned
routing sits at that floor, so each slice state with weights on is a mean
over about one fifth as many effective tokens as with weights off, and
over four resamplings of the same surface the slice states move 1.9–2.3x
more relative to their spread; no slice is dominated by a few large cells
(ten cells never carry more than 18% of a slice's mass), and slices routed
to large cells are not poorer in tokens than others, so neither saturation
nor starvation holds. The two components of the price separate by their
dependence on cell count, because estimator variance shrinks as more cells
are drawn and mesh-pattern content does not (@sec-nb-bench-verdict). On
the uniform sampler the weights-off ÷ weights-on ratio on DrivAerML rises
from 0.89 at 2,500 cells to 0.98 at 40,000, so the car price is variance
and is nearly gone at the highest count; at 35 HiLiftAeroML cases (0.88)
and on the fixed-angle split (0.87) the ratio is flat across the same
sixteen-fold range, which variance cannot produce, so the wing price is
mesh-pattern content. That content is what the weights-off ablation
learned instead of the physics: evaluated on the area-proportional
sampler, where the quadrature weights are nearly constant, the
uniform-trained weights-off checkpoints collapse to errors of 0.66–1.29
(worse than predicting zero) against 0.10–0.51 with weights on, a 2–7x
inversion on all three datasets, and weights-on's error keeps falling with
cell count while weights-off's stays flat
(`results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json`, float32,
two seeds). Weights off is therefore an ablation that prices the measure
semantics, never a configuration (@sec-principle).

**The reference frame's price on the wings is the mesher pattern that a
plain-mean frame carries, and it is paid where validation geometries recur
in training.** The reference configuration builds every invariant from
relative positions and the total surface measure, with no centroid, no
sample statistic and no per-dataset length anywhere (@sec-mt2). Against
the constant-gauge variant, which centres on the plain sample mean with a
constant reference length, it costs 0% on DrivAerML (0.0552 against
0.0557), 1% at four training geometries (0.2520 against 0.2496), 5% at 21
geometries (0.1066 against 0.1014), 11% at 35 and 210 random cases (0.1529
against 0.1377; 0.0716 against 0.0643) and 14.5% at the fixed angle
(0.0398 against 0.0348, three seeds; @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict). Two
diagnostics with an exact full-geometry frame settle what the price is:
given the exact geometric centroid and scale of the whole wing as global
data and every positional seed, ISLA pays 14–16% at 35 cases and 21% at
the fixed angle, more than the frame-free reference, so the price is not
positional information lost with the seeds but the mesh-density content
of the plain-mean frame, which is displaced from the geometric centroid by
0.13 body lengths on the wings and 0.03 on the cars
(@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict, @sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict). The
ladder reads as recurrence: the price is 1–5% on the two rungs whose
validation geometries never appear in training and 11% on the two rungs
where they recur, because an estimated centre and scale give every token an
absolute position on a wing that is reusable when the wing returns and a
liability when it does not. The fixed angle is the one never-seen-geometry
rung where the reference still pays, and the reading that a single drive
direction makes the mesher's refinement pattern along leading edges and
flaps a geometric cue that transfers within the wing family is consistent
with every rung and not separately tested (@sec-open-questions). The scale
choice is not the cost: with the total-measure scale the reference pays
less at the fixed angle than the relative frame with a constant reference
length (14.5% against 22%). Against the similarity-gauge variant, which
centres on the Horvitz–Thompson centroid and scales by the RMS radius, the
reference is the more accurate ISLA at four geometries (0.94x), at parity
at the fixed angle (1.00x, three seeds), at 21 geometries (1.02x) and on
DrivAerML (1.02x), and loses 3–9% where geometries recur (1.03x at 35
cases, 1.09x at 210). The
reference stays by the principle of @sec-principle, and its price is
stated per rung.

The interior standings sort the same way on a single car (one car, 64
views, float32 at the training count of 10,000 queries;
@sec-nb-overfit-interior): the velocity lead is identical with the data
fixed, so it is capacity; the eddy-viscosity deficit is wider with the
data fixed, so it is capacity too and more cars will not close it; and the
full-data pressure standing reverses on one car, so what pressure lead the
interacting configuration has at full data is generalization across cars,
not representation (@sec-interior-open).

### Regime extrapolation fails for every architecture tested {#sec-limits-regime}

**Neither architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary, and ISLA's
structure does not change that** (@sec-regime-extrapolation). The readout is
d = (pressure rel-L2 on the sealed out-of-regime test set) / (pressure rel-L2
on in-regime validation cases). Trained at angles of attack up to 12° and
tested at 14° and above, or trained pre-stall and tested post-stall, both
architectures lose about a factor of ten, and the out-of-regime errors
(0.24–0.33) are worse than either architecture reaches from 35 in-regime
cases (constant-gauge ISLA 0.138, unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.111). ISLA
keeps the lower absolute error against the physical-drive GeoTransolver,
which has the smaller d because its in-regime floor is higher; both
GeoTransolver regime runs consumed the physical velocity
(@sec-part-baseline), so the ordering and the ratios are physical-drive
measurements. Coverage of the regime, not architecture, governs this axis.

Whether GeoTransolver's smaller ratio comes from its raw-coordinate inputs
was tested directly: ISLA with a raw-coordinate channel appended to its seed
invariants, which breaks the SE(3) contract, trained on the stall split with
two seeds and evaluated once on the sealed post-stall test. The
preregistered bands were: raw coordinates carry the ratio if d is 11.0 or
below with out-of-regime pressure below 0.245; they do not if d is 12.0 or
above or pressure is 0.255 or above. Measured: d = 12.7/13.3, against 12.5
for ISLA and 9.3 for GeoTransolver, with sealed-test pressure
0.262/0.267. The falsifier fires: raw-coordinate inputs do not give ISLA
GeoTransolver's smaller ratio, and no mechanism for it has been isolated.
Because ISLA has the lower absolute error on both sides of the boundary,
there is no transfer advantage to explain and the thread is closed.

### Interior accuracy: ahead on velocity, behind on pressure and eddy viscosity; the passive decode trails by 3.1x {#sec-limits-interior}

**On the boundary → interior task, ISLA's reference configuration, query
tokens with the signed distance on the relative frame, is more accurate
than GeoTransolver-volume on interior velocity (0.73x in float32) and less
accurate on interior pressure (1.07x) and eddy viscosity (1.14x) at a
third of the parameters; the similarity-gauge interior variant matches it
on pressure and velocity and trails on eddy viscosity (1.27x, three
seeds); at matched parameters (hidden 344, 27.6M) that variant leads on
pressure (0.97x) and velocity (0.68x) and trails on eddy viscosity
(1.18x); without the signed distance it trails on every field (1.2x, 1.3x,
1.6x); ISLA's passive, query-independent decode trails by 3.1x on
pressure, and that deficit ratio grows with distance from the wall**
(@sec-interior). The setting is DrivAerML volume fields at 10,000 interior
query points; ISLA predicts them from the surface sample and the queries'
signed distances, GeoTransolver-volume from the interior points themselves
as interacting tokens carrying the signed distance, at 27.6M parameters
against ISLA's 8.9M. Four limits. GeoTransolver-volume fed the physical
freestream velocity instead of the unit direction changes by under 2% on
every field (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), so the interior ratios are not an
input-scale artifact, and the comparison is not resource-matched
(@sec-interior-task). The full-data standings only partly extend to small
data: at 54 and 109 training cars GeoTransolver-volume leads the
query-token configuration without the signed distance by 1.3x on interior
pressure, wider than the 1.2x by which it leads ISLA on the DrivAerML
surface below full data; with the signed distance the pressure deficit is
1.19x at 54 cars and 1.18x at 109, velocity is an ISLA lead from 109 cars
up (0.94x at 54, 0.83x at 109, 0.73x at 435), and eddy viscosity stays
1.3–1.5x in GeoTransolver-volume's favour throughout (@sec-interior-open).
The interacting decode's prediction depends on the joint query set: on the
similarity-gauge variant, pressure error is 0.0753 at 2,000 queries,
0.0547 at the training count of 10,000 and 0.0531 at 20,000, training over
a range of counts reduces the dependence by about 40% at a 3.7% cost and
does not remove it, and the passive decode's dependence is exactly zero, so
the interacting configuration is deployed at the training count
(@sec-interior-companion, @sec-nb-qcount-verdict). And the 3.1x is the
cost of the complete passive configuration as built, a separate four-block
read decoder without the signed-distance input; a passive decode at
matched depth and inputs (twelve read blocks, an interacting support set
carrying the signed distance) costs 1.43x on pressure and 2.41x on eddy
viscosity, so query independence itself has a measured price on this task
(@sec-interior-query-independence). For the passive decode, the deficit
ratio is 2.5x near the wall and 3.3–5.4x in the far bands, while 95% of the
excess squared error on the sampled points lies within 5 cm of the wall, so
the ratio's growth does not identify a missing mechanism
(@sec-interior-distance). Equivariant latent tokens placed off each slice
anchor along its mean normal make the passive decode worse by 1.43x, and
an exact boundary-integral prior is not an option either: on DrivAerML a
potential-flow oracle scores worse than predicting each case's mean
pressure, because the dominant physics is separation
(@sec-interior-negatives).

The open item on the interior is the eddy-viscosity gap, 14% for the
reference configuration on the recipe's standardized viscosity metric,
which is not a physical percentage. Its location is known: on the
matched-parameter similarity-gauge variant, ISLA leads GeoTransolver-volume
on eddy viscosity everywhere within 0.4 body lengths of the surface, around
the car and upstream, and the entire deficit is the far wake beyond 0.4
body lengths downstream, 2.2% of the query points (@sec-interior-open).
Anchor geometry does not close it (wake tokens on the drive axis close a
fifth of the far-band gap, within the seed spread; latent volume tokens
make it worse), a measure-consistent oversampling of the far wake at
training time makes every field worse under uniform deployment and cannot
separate under-sampling from the query-distribution swap it introduces
(@sec-nb-farwake-verdict), surface-patch local features on the query
tokens and query-density or query-neighbour channels do not close it and
the latter two read the discretization and are excluded by @sec-principle,
and a width increase to 256 narrows it to 1.17x without closing it. The
single-car test identifies the gap as a capacity limit: with the data fixed
the eddy-viscosity ratio widens to 1.64x, so more training cars will not
close it (@sec-nb-overfit-interior). The reference frame with the
corrected boundary measure narrows it from 1.27x to 1.14x while leaving
pressure and velocity unchanged; the two changes were made together and
the gain is not attributed between them (@sec-nb-relint-verdict). Two
facts bound the query-token configuration itself: its query weights scale
with the geometric mean of the surface weights, so refining the surface
sample or changing the number of queries changes its prediction (4–9% on
small random models; on trained checkpoints the standings hold at or above
the training query count and are consumed below it,
@sec-interior-companion); and DrivAerML's hybrid RANS/LES closure makes the
modeled viscosity depend on the mesh, so a local aggregation over
neighbouring interior points may recover discretization rather than
physics, a reading that the null of the density and neighbour channels
weakens without settling.

### Exact query independence costs 3.0–3.7x and is not in the reference configuration {#sec-limits-query-independence}

**ISLA's surface predictions in the reference configuration depend weakly on
which other points are sampled; making them exactly independent costs
3.0–3.7x in accuracy, so every surface checkpoint behind the headline
results is the interacting configuration** (@sec-query-independence). Query
independence means the prediction at a point does not change when the other
queried points change. In the reference configuration the heads read from
the interacting encoder tokens, and swapping the companion set moves a
point's prediction by about 7% (2% for GeoTransolver at a shared 5,000-cell
prefix). The optional query-independent configuration replaces the heads
with passive read blocks; it is exactly independent in fp64 and 3.0–3.7x
less accurate on DrivAerML surface pressure: 3.5–3.7x against the
interacting reference at the same learning rate, 3.0–3.3x against the
6,500-token control at matched memory.
Evaluate-anywhere semantics is a contract with a measured price. The
interior confirms it at matched depth: a passive decode that reads through
twelve blocks from an interacting support set of 5,000 surface tokens
carrying the signed distance scores 0.078 / 0.107 / 0.269 on pressure,
velocity and eddy viscosity against 0.055 / 0.080 / 0.112 for the
interacting query-token configuration, 1.43x, 1.34x and 2.41x, past the
preregistered falsifier of 0.060 on pressure; depth buys 13% and the
support 12% on pressure and neither anything on eddy viscosity. What the
interacting queries provide is computation at the requested points through
every encoder layer, not geometric context, so the passive route is closed
for ISLA at matched depth and inputs
(`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/d1_verdict_2026-09-10.json`).
Training over a range of request sizes reduces the interacting decode's
dependence by about 40% at a 3.7% accuracy cost and does not remove it
(@sec-nb-qcount-verdict), so the dependence is partly intrinsic, and
deployment at the training count is the rule.

### Cross-family transfer is a data property {#sec-limits-transfer}

**Neither ISLA nor GeoTransolver transfers zero-shot across vehicle
families; what moves cross-family error is the diversity of the training
data** (@tbl-frontier in @sec-full-data). The failure is not identical across
the two architectures: on the held-out fastback family the models trained on
DrivAerML alone score, in float32 on two seeds, 0.61 for the unit-drive
GeoTransolver and 0.79 for the constant-gauge ISLA at its reference
learning rate (0.98 for the same construction trained at 3e-3; 1.0 is the
mean predictor), so ISLA's zero-shot failure is 29% worse than
GeoTransolver's, but neither is usable, and a second training family moves
both to 0.11–0.13. Few-shot adaptation separates them further: fine-tuned
on 20 labelled fastback cases for 1,000 steps, the unit-drive GeoTransolver
reaches 0.128 against 0.186 trained from scratch on those cases, while ISLA
reaches 0.187 against 0.198 (float32, matched learning rate;
research/transfer_program, #sec-nb-campc-t3-verdict), so what GeoTransolver
learns on DrivAerML is a better starting point for a new family than what
ISLA learns there (the two source checkpoints differ in drive input and
learning rate as well as architecture, a caveat stated with the result;
the ISLA fine-tune's start from its trained weights is verified: the
source model passed through the fine-tuning loader at zero learning rate
reproduces its own zero-shot error to four digits). The
cleanest form of the finding is at the two ends of adaptation: on the first
batch of fastback cases the pretrained ISLA's training loss is 2.5x lower
than a random initialization's (0.194 against 0.477) and the pretrained
GeoTransolver's 1.6x lower (0.176 against 0.278), so the two architectures'
DrivAerML knowledge is worth about the same at step zero; after 1,000
matched-rate steps ISLA's head start has shrunk to 6% while GeoTransolver's
has grown to 31%. No single ISLA ingredient carries that deficit: retraining
with 128 or 512 anchors, with raw seeds in place of the drive-relative
invariants, with the similarity gauge at either rate or with the measure weights off
moves the zero-shot fastback error nowhere near GeoTransolver's (best arm
0.767 against 0.788 and 0.612; three seeds each, spreads up to 0.30;
@sec-nb-xfam-verdict), so the cross-family question is a data question.
Diversity at a fixed label budget is a trade, not a free
lunch: with 435 training cases split 218 DrivAerML and 217 estate instead of
all DrivAerML, ISLA's zero-shot fastback error falls from 0.788 to 0.128 and
GeoTransolver's from 0.612 to 0.115 (drag error from above 150% to 16% and
13%), while in-family DrivAerML error rises from 0.0557 to 0.0737 for ISLA
(+32%) and from 0.0504 to 0.0598 for GeoTransolver (+19%) (float32, seed
means; `research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t2_2026-09-10.json`,
#sec-nb-campc-t2-verdict). The preregistered bar, a 30% drop at no more than
10% in-family cost, fails on the cost side for both architectures. Four
protocol-matched runs trained on the 218 DrivAerML cars alone split the
cost: for ISLA, halving the source data costs 1.23x (0.0557 to 0.0683) and
adding the 217 estate cars on top costs a further 1.08x (to 0.0737); for
GeoTransolver the factors are 1.14x and 1.04x. Most of the in-family cost
is therefore what any halving of the source data costs, the sibling family
itself costs 4–8% at a 50% share, and ISLA pays more on both factors, in the
same direction as the few-shot result. At a fixed
label budget, half the labels on the target's sibling family buy the target
family almost entirely and cost the source about what halving its data
costs, plus 4–8% for the mixing. Two further facts
bound the trade. The mixing cost grows with the foreign share for ISLA and
not for GeoTransolver: with all 435 DrivAerML cars kept and 794 estate cars
added (a 65% foreign share, source not halved) ISLA's in-family error rises
17% (0.0557 to 0.0652) and GeoTransolver's 4% (0.0504 to 0.0525), against 8%
and 4% at the 50% share; and the extra 577 estate cars buy the fastback
cases only 6% (ISLA) and 9% (GeoTransolver) over the 217-car mix, so
coverage of a sibling family saturates within a few hundred cars. A per-case
family flag (a boundary scalar for ISLA, a seventh functional channel for
GeoTransolver) changes nothing on the held-out family or in-family (within
the seed spread), so the mismatch is coverage, not identification
(`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t1_2026-09-10.json`).
With the zero-shot force error of 1.6x and the constant-gauge variant's
density collapse, this is the third independent sign that ISLA's learned
representation is family-specific. The similarity gauge, which removes the
constant-gauge variant's sampling-density failure (@sec-robustness-density),
leaves zero-shot transfer unchanged. A claim of family-portable surface
physics from any of these architectures would need a corpus in which
geometry, pose, scale and regime vary one at a time (@sec-open-questions).

## Open questions, and what would settle each {#sec-open-questions}

Each question has, or acquires before it runs, a preregistered prediction
in readout units and a
falsifier,^[Preregistrations: @sec-nb-udrvl-prereg,
@sec-nb-w2-prereg, @sec-nb-deflection-prereg,
@sec-nb-g5-prereg, @sec-nb-mom2-prereg.] and
the measurements that remain open are listed in @sec-program-status.
Unless stated, the readout is the pressure rel-L2 of
@sec-limits-data-efficiency and the ratio is baseline ÷ ISLA, so above 1
favours ISLA; the older preregistrations were written in ISLA/GT, the
inverse, and each threshold below is labelled with its direction. The first
question is the one whose answer would most change the book: it decides
whether ISLA has any surface-accuracy advantage anywhere once the inputs
are matched.

- **Does ISLA have an accuracy advantage at any HiLiftAeroML rung against
  unit-drive baselines?** GeoTransolver fed the unit freestream direction
  at every rung of the ladder, with the frozen protocol and the reference
  runs' learning rates (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). At each rung, ISLA has an
  advantage only if baseline ÷ ISLA is at least 1.10 with ISLA lower on at
  least two thirds of the validation cases (and on at least 12 of 18
  geometries on the geometry rungs); parity is 0.95–1.05; the baseline is
  ahead at 0.90 or below. Prediction: the unit-drive baselines match or
  beat ISLA at every rung. Measured at six of seven rungs, the prediction
  holds: GeoTransolver 0.80x at 35 cases (Transolver 0.83x), 0.83x at 210
  (Transolver 0.91x), 0.84x at 510 (Transolver 0.90x; both lower on 168 of
  180 cases), 0.76x at 4 geometries, 0.92x at 21 geometries, 0.78x at the
  fixed angle (@sec-nb-udrvl-210-verdict, @sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict,
  @sec-nb-udrvl-geo210-verdict, @sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict,
  @sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict). The 1,260-case rung is the one not yet
  measured.
- **If an advantage survives at some rung, where on the wing does it
  live, and is gap geometry the information that carries it?** The
  gap-distance stratification of @sec-mechanism, re-run against the
  unit-drive checkpoints at that rung (localization: supported if the
  near-gap-band ratio is at least 1.5x the rest-of-surface ratio, falsified
  if uniform within 1.15x), followed by a perturbation test (gap-region
  points removed or perturbed against matched-area controls on a fixed
  query set) for the information question. Both are conditional on the
  first question leaving something to explain.
- **Is the flattening a protocol floor?** Both architectures at 1,260 cases
  with 20,000 rather than 10,000 sampled points per case. If the floor is
  the protocol's, both improve by a similar factor (within 5 percentage
  points). If GeoTransolver improves by 10 percentage points or more than
  ISLA, the floor is ISLA's. The GeoTransolver arm is a physical-drive run;
  its reading is about the floor, not the ordering.
- **The deflection split** trains on the 80% of geometries with the lower
  flap-and-slat deflection and evaluates once on the 20% with the most
  aggressive settings (held out per checkpoint, not a program-level
  confirmation, @sec-limits-validation; bars in @sec-nb-deflection-prereg,
  written in ISLA/GT). Its GeoTransolver arm is physical-drive, so the
  ISLA arm is a measurement of ISLA's error across a geometry-parameter
  boundary and not a comparison of architectures unless a unit-drive
  baseline is run on the same split.
- **Why does the reference frame pay at the fixed angle?** The fixed-angle
  split is the one never-seen-geometry rung where the frame-free reference
  pays for leaving the plain-mean frame (14.5% against 1–5% on the other
  never-seen rungs, @sec-limits-mechanism). The full-geometry-frame
  diagnostic rules out positional information lost with the seeds; the
  reading left standing, that at a single drive direction the mesher's
  refinement pattern along leading edges and flaps becomes a geometric cue
  that transfers within the wing family, is consistent with every rung and
  not separately tested. A test would hold the geometry fixed and vary the
  mesher: if the constant-gauge variant's fixed-angle advantage over the
  reference vanishes on a re-meshed validation set, the cue is the mesher's;
  if it persists, the reading is wrong.
- **What is the force error against the full surface?** Lift and drag
  from 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000 sampled cells and from the full surface,
  labels and predictions, on a preselected set of validation cases at 35 and
  1,260 training cases. ISLA's 3% figure at 35 cases holds against the full
  surface if the full-surface error is within 1.5 percentage points of the
  sampled-cell error; if the sampled-cell reference itself deviates from the
  full-surface integral by more than the model error, the reported force
  errors are quadrature-limited and are restated against the full surface.
  The baselines' 35-case force errors in @sec-data-efficiency (8–17%) are
  physical-drive measurements; the unit-drive baselines' forces are not yet
  reduced.
- **Is a second-moment channel worth having?** The expressivity benchmark
  on the first-moment collision family (@sec-mt2-contracts): ISLA with a
  per-slice second-moment contraction, against the base model and the
  local-distance channel, scored by whether a linear probe on the
  common-component output separates the two arrangement families; bars in
  @sec-nb-mom2-prereg. It decides whether the documented representation
  limitation is cheap to remove before any larger geometric-algebra backbone
  is considered.
- **Is there a stronger independent baseline?** Every baseline in this
  book is from the Transolver family. AB-UPT (an anchored neural-field
  decoder; TMLR, arXiv 2502.09692) is the published architecture whose
  design most directly contradicts the interior finding here, that
  accuracy needed the queries to interact; AB-GATr (arXiv 2605.18816) is
  the scalable equivariant comparator for ISLA's combination of symmetry
  and accuracy; regularized family adaptation (arXiv 2605.27968) tests
  whether the zero-shot cross-family failure is cheaper to close by
  adapting than by collecting a family from scratch; and Transolver++ is
  the template's `plus` option, a cheap control that is not a reproduction
  of that paper. Each is a candidate node, to be run under this protocol
  with the freestream at unit scale for every model; published numbers
  on other splits are not a comparison with ISLA.
- **Does boundary self-identification help ISLA?** The largest measured
  industrial gain of the exact-kernel MeshTransformer (@sec-interior) came from a trace
  formulation that let each boundary token identify its own cell in the
  readout, so that a prediction at a surface point had an explicit term from
  that point's own cell rather than only from the pooled field. ISLA's
  routing has no analogous explicit term: the heads read each surface
  point's encoder token, but after twelve layers of slice routing that token
  holds whatever the routing mixed into it, and nothing in the readout marks
  the point's own position, normal and area apart from the field. The test
  is a single-factor addition of an own-token readout channel to ISLA,
  everything else frozen, at 35 and 1,260 HiLift cases, two seeds. Falsified
  if it moves neither rung by more than the two-seed spread; a gain at 35
  cases only would say the term is a small-data aid, at both rungs that
  ISLA's readout is missing a general ingredient.
- **Which generalization axes does structure buy, one at a time?** A 3D
  RANS corpus generated with counterfactual twin draws per factor (pose,
  scale, Reynolds number, layout, mesh), so each axis is tested exactly.
  Preregistered: on pose twins GeoTransolver without a freestream frame
  fails by 5x or more and canonicalized GeoTransolver matches ISLA within
  1.05x; on scale twins at fixed Reynolds number across 0.02–20 m (the
  first real test of the similarity gauge) GeoTransolver exceeds 2x at a 10x
  scale change; on Reynolds twins no architecture transfers a decade of Re
  better than another; mesh twins set the floor below which no difference
  is reportable. The arms are void unless twin draws are adopted at
  generation time, which is why the preregistration precedes the corpus.

## Engineering directions {#sec-future}

**Cost.** On the recipe's compiled path, with both models compiled as the
recipe runs them (one GB300, bfloat16, 10,000 tokens, batch 1), ISLA's
step is 47 ms at 1.30 GiB with the geometry recompute on, 1.05x
GeoTransolver's 45 ms at 2.70 GiB, and 39 ms at 1.94 GiB without the
recompute (0.86x). At 40,000 tokens the default compiled ISLA takes 119 ms
against GeoTransolver's 53 ms (2.2x); the exact fused geometry kernel
(opt-in `geo_kernel="fused"`) brings it to 52 ms at 4.5 GiB against
10.0 GiB. Every stage but the MLP is memory-bound, and the relational
invariants carry 61% of the traffic, which is why the fused kernel and the
recompute pay (@sec-mt2-cost, @sec-nb-kernel-study).^[Measurement records:
@sec-nb-geo-pool-memory, @sec-nb-geo-recompute.] Two exact rewrites set
the memory figure. The relational readback pools the softmax slice mixture
before the affine projection, so the activation saved per layer for the
backward pass is (points × 8) rather than (points × slices × hidden/2),
and the remaining per-slice geometry is rebuilt inside the backward pass
rather than stored (2.3x less memory for 1.16x step time on the eager
path); the rewrites compute the same function (fp64 maximum difference
4e-15). The fused kernel is a validated speed option rather than part of
the frozen protocol: it is opt-in, the default path is the bitwise
reference, and the fused path's output differs from it by a relative L2
below 6e-7, at the roundoff floor (@sec-nb-geo-compile).
The gap below GeoTransolver's footprint is headroom for more tokens per
case or a wider model at a step time within 5% of GeoTransolver's at
10,000 tokens.

**Measure weights: a correctness requirement with an in-distribution
price.** ISLA weights each surface point by its cell area in the slice
routing and the pooled anchors, which is what makes its slice states
estimates of surface integrals and its predictions consistent under
refinement. Under uniform 10,000-point sampling the weights cost accuracy
in distribution, 5–10% at 35 HiLiftAeroML cases (draw-dependent) and 2.9%
on DrivAerML, and @sec-limits-mechanism locates the price: estimator
variance, which shrinks with cell count and is nearly gone at 40,000 cells
on the cars, plus mesh-pattern content on the wings, which does not shrink
and collapses under area-proportional sampling to errors worse than
predicting zero. The weights-off ablation also degrades 19x under the 10:1
sampling bias against 1.2x for the reference, so what it gains in
distribution it pays several times over off it. Weights off is therefore an
ablation that prices the measure semantics, never a configuration
(@sec-principle). The principled target for the in-distribution price is
the sampler or a variance-reduced consistent quadrature, not the weights.

**Sampling conventions.** No architecture is consistent across sampling
conventions at 10,000 cells: trained under uniform-over-cells sampling and
scored under area-proportional sampling, or the reverse, the
measure-weighted ISLA pays 1.5–1.9x and the released baselines 3–7x, and
every architecture trained on both conventions handles both at no cost
(@sec-nb-mix-verdict). For the measure-weighted ISLA the penalty is a
finite-sample effect and converges: the swap ratio falls from 2.9x at 2,500
cells to 1.45x at 10,000 and 1.05x at 40,000 (the reverse direction 2.7x
to 1.21x), while the baselines' 3–7x does not move
(@sec-nb-mix-refinement;
`results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_mixarea_2026-09-11.json`).
Mesher transfer is therefore a property of the training data at the
recipe's resolution, and of the measure-consistent estimator in the
fine-mesh limit, which at 40,000 cells is within 5% of reached. The
sampler is under the model's control in training and not at inference, so
consistency under a sampler the model did not choose is the property that
matters for deployment, and it is the reference frame's (@sec-consistency-bench).

## What would change the recommendation {#sec-review-roads}

ISLA's reference configuration, the frame-free relative frame with the
total-measure scale, is not recommended over GeoTransolver or Transolver
for surface pressure where the deployment mesher matches the training
mesher and geometries arrive in a known frame. On HiLiftAeroML the
unit-drive baselines are more accurate at every rung measured
(@sec-part-baseline): at 35 training cases GeoTransolver and Transolver
score 0.111 and 0.115 against the reference's 0.1529 (0.73x and 0.75x),
and the ratios against the constant-gauge variant are 0.76–0.92x on the
other five rungs. On smooth single-body families such as DrivAerML,
GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate on the surface below full data
(physical drive, which on this dataset is not a handicap) and the released
GeoTransolver and Transolver score 0.0503 and 0.0517 against the
reference's 0.0552 at full data in float32; GeoTransolver or Transolver is
the recommendation on DrivAerML surface pressure at every size. The
reference's price against the constant-gauge variant is 0% on DrivAerML,
1–5% on the never-seen-geometry count rungs, 11% where validation
geometries recur in training and 14.5% at the fixed angle; against the
similarity-gauge variant it is 3–9% where geometries recur and nothing
elsewhere. The reference stays by the principle of @sec-principle, since
the price on the wings is the mesher pattern the plain-mean frame carries
(@sec-limits-mechanism), and for a fixed fleet of shapes that recur
between training and deployment the two variants are the cheaper ISLA on
HiLiftAeroML by that margin.

Where geometries arrive in arbitrary poses the contracts earn accuracy:
on DrivAerML with every training and validation case in its own random
SO(3) pose, ISLA scores 0.0566 (1.01x its canonical error) against 0.0602
for GeoTransolver with SO(3) augmentation (1.20x its canonical) and 0.0676
for Transolver with augmentation (1.31x), a 6% and 19% lead in float32
that reverses the canonical-frame ordering (research/transfer_program,
#sec-nb-campb-verdict; GeoTransolver without augmentation scores 0.0631).
Elsewhere what ISLA offers on the surface is its contracts:
exact rotation and translation covariance without a frame estimate or a
freestream direction at inference, which a canonicalized GeoTransolver
matches only where a frame can be estimated (@sec-pose); a
query-independent configuration at a measured 3.0–3.7x accuracy cost
(@sec-query-independence); and consistency under sampling. Consistency
splits the recommendation. On accuracy the released baselines lead, and
measure-weighted pooling does not change that: GeoTransolver and
Transolver with the surface measure in their slice pooling score 0.0498
and 0.0522 on DrivAerML and 0.85x and 0.88x of the constant-gauge ISLA at
35 HiLift cases (@sec-nb-mw-verdict). On consistency the frame decides,
not the pooling: every architecture that centres its coordinates on a
statistic of the sampled points collapses 10–16x under a 10:1
sampling-density bias when the frame is taken from the biased sample
(released GeoTransolver 12x, Transolver 10–13x, their measure-weighted
variants 14–16x, the constant-gauge ISLA 12x; @sec-nb-mw-postcenter), and
only frames that do not read the sample hold: the reference at 1.2x, and
the measure-weighted baselines given a Horvitz–Thompson estimate of the
geometric centroid as their datapipe frame at 1.03–1.04x
(@sec-nb-mwaw-verdict; `results/mwaw_2026-09-11.json`). The consistency
advantage is therefore a property of the frame, not of the architecture.
The measure-weighted, Horvitz–Thompson-centred GeoTransolver and
Transolver that match ISLA on consistency are research variants built for
this comparison, to locate the property; the released GeoTransolver and
Transolver are stable, in use and published, and are not modified
(@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines), so measure weighting and a
sample-free frame reach users through ISLA. The fair comparison reports the
released baselines as the deployable comparison and their
measure-consistent variants as the diagnostic. Under refinement and across
sampling laws no configuration is consistent at 10,000 cells; the
measure-weighted ISLA arms converge toward the uniform answer under the
area-proportional sampler, 2.9x → 1.45x → 1.05x from 2,500 to 40,000
cells, while the released baselines stay at 3–7x (@sec-consistency-bench,
@sec-nb-mix-refinement).

So on surface pressure at the reference size GeoTransolver or Transolver is
the more accurate choice wherever the deployment mesher matches the
training mesher and the pose is known, and ISLA is the choice wherever the
sampling may differ from the training sampling, where geometries arrive in
arbitrary poses, on the interior at matched parameters, or where memory at
scale binds. Its learning-rate robustness on DrivAerML (1.55x degradation
at 1e-2 against 4–14x for GeoTransolver, @sec-robustness-lr) is a fact
about training, not an accuracy claim. On the interior, ISLA's reference
configuration leads GeoTransolver-volume on velocity (0.73x) at a third of
the parameters and trails on pressure (1.07x) and eddy viscosity (1.14x),
at or above the training query count (@sec-interior); the
similarity-gauge interior variant at matched parameters leads on pressure
as well (0.97x) and trails only on eddy viscosity (1.18x); the unit-drive
control of GeoTransolver-volume changed nothing (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict).
GeoTransolver-volume is the choice where eddy viscosity is the target
field, or where the training set is small and pressure is the target. Two
outcomes would change this.

**ISLA regains an accuracy claim on HiLiftAeroML** if the unit-drive
GeoTransolver at 1,260 cases leaves it ahead by the preregistered margin
(baseline ÷ ISLA at least 1.10 with ISLA lower on two thirds of the cases;
@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). That rung and its mechanism would then be the
program's only surface-accuracy claim, stated against the unit-drive
baseline, and the localization and perturbation instruments of
@sec-open-questions would run there. The prediction, which has held at
six of seven rungs, is that this does not happen, and the six measured
rungs already fix the recommendation for every training-set size below
1,260 cases.

**The interior recommendation becomes unconditional for ISLA** only if a
principled configuration closes the eddy-viscosity gap (within 1.10x of
GeoTransolver-volume) at the reference width without moving pressure or
velocity by more than 5%. The single-car test identifies the gap as
capacity (@sec-nb-overfit-interior), the far wake beyond 0.4 body lengths
carries the whole of it, and anchor geometry, training-time sampling and
query-side inputs do not close it (@sec-interior-open); a width increase to
27.6M parameters leaves it at 1.18x, so at matched parameters the
recommendation is already ISLA on pressure and velocity and
GeoTransolver-volume on eddy viscosity.

If neither fires, the recommendation stands as written, with the bounds of
this chapter attached: the program's ISLA-specific claims are exact
covariance and its 6% and 19% lead in arbitrary poses, the passive
query-independent decode at its measured price, consistency under sampling
as a property of the reference frame, the interior velocity lead, and the
cost figures of @sec-mt2-cost, and no surface-accuracy claim in a known
frame.
